public_rationale: Reporting supports losses on heavy Copilot users in early 2023, and GitHub acknowledged an unsustainable billing model in April 2026. Neither establishes that users could exceed their fees in actual inference costs every month for three years. The reported profitability announcement also cautions against treating heavy-user subsidies as service-wide losses.
limitations: The original WSJ article could not be read; its figures are represented through contemporaneous reporting.
The relevant GitHub announcement was not extractable through read_page.
No standalone historical subscriber-cost accounts were obtained.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: For three years Microsoft let GitHub Copilot users burn more in tokens each month than their subscriptions cost.

statement.excerpt: While Copilot might not be “...the same product it was a year ago,” very little has changed about the underlying economic mismatch: that Microsoft was allowing users to burn more than their subscription costs in tokens every single month for three years.

from_speaker: more than their subscription costs in tokens
every single month for three years
our_interpretation: The ordinary reading is that heavy users could incur inference costs exceeding their monthly fees. It does not require every subscriber to do so.
Three years means approximately the three years preceding publication, represented as April 28, 2023 through April 28, 2026.
The surrounding discussion of subsidies and losses makes Microsoft's actual costs the relevant measure. Retail API-equivalent prices alone are insufficient.
The accounting basis is estimate because Zitron explicitly relies on press reporting about internal costs.
criteria.support_condition: Historical plan allowances and credible actual-cost records establish that users could consume more than their subscription fees in each month throughout the stated interval.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable records establish an intervening period when enforced allowances prevented subscribers from incurring inference costs above their fees. Overall service profitability alone would not establish this.

evidence.locator: Opening discussion of the WSJ's early-2023 figures
evidence.explanation: The article reports a $10 monthly fee and losses on heavy users in early 2023. This supports the historical premise but does not establish costs in every subsequent month.

evidence.locator: GitHub chief product officer's explanation of the billing change
evidence.explanation: GitHub acknowledged cost pressure under its existing billing model. The statement supplies neither monthly per-user costs nor evidence covering the entire three-year interval.

This conference account reports profitability, which challenges any inference that the whole service continuously lost money. A profitable service can still subsidize individual heavy users, so it does not contradict the contracted claim.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Dated plan limits and actual inference-cost records covering the intervening months, or records showing a period when costs could not exceed subscription fees.
